# Why does a market maker earn anything?

*You'll need the book, the spread, taking and making, and fills (chapter 2), and the fair value (chapter 3).*

## The story

Put our template alone into Prosperity 3's round 1 and it makes 72,674 credits over three days. Put a second copy of the same
bot into the same market, quoting the same prices, and each copy makes about 41 thousand: 41,352 and 41,848. With two
copies beside it, each makes 27 to 30 thousand (@fig-copies). Nothing about the market changed except that someone
else was offering the same thing at the same price
[(`data/copies.csv`; the method in `IDEAS.md`, "The template against copies of itself")]{.src}.

![The same bot alone, against one copy of itself and against two, on Prosperity 3's round 1. Data: `data/copies.csv`,
from `arena.backtest ... --vs python/bots/template.py`.](../figures/f06_copies.png){#fig-copies
fig-alt="Bar chart: alone 73 thousand; with one copy 41 and 42 thousand; with two copies 27, 29 and 30 thousand."}

On Prosperity 4's Osmium the same measurement against other teams' bots gives the cleanest picture: the spread there is
a pie of 55 to 62 thousand credits a round, and the bots split it. Our template kept 45 to 51% against one rival and 20% against
three [(`IDEAS.md`, "The template against the teams' P4 traders in one market")]{.src}. A market maker's income is a
rent, and rents are shared.

## The idea

### The spread is a fee for immediacy

Someone who wants to trade *now* crosses the book and pays the spread: they buy at the ask, above the mid, or sell at
the bid, below it. Someone willing to wait posts an order and lets the hurried come to them. The market maker is the
one who waits on both sides at once. Each time a taker buys from its ask and another sells to its bid, it has bought
low and sold high by the width of its quotes, without needing any view of where the price is going.

@fig-round-trip shows this at small scale, the template's first 400 steps on one product of the Varde rehearsal. Most
of its fills are passive, sells above the mid and buys below it, with some takes among them; its position swings between short 9 and
long 6 and keeps coming back to zero; and its profit climbs in small steps, about €4 over 400 steps, while the price
itself drifts down.

![A market maker's first 400 steps: LUMEN, the Varde rehearsal's session 1. Top, the mid and our fills; middle, our
position; bottom, PnL valued at the mid. Data: `data/round_trip.csv`, from the rehearsal portal's fills.](../figures/f05_round_trip.png){#fig-round-trip
fig-alt="Three panels over 400 steps: the price drifts down from 101.5 to 101.2 euros with our buys below and sells above it; our position swings between minus 9 and plus 6 lots; our profit rises steadily to about 4 euros."}

### What can go wrong: the price moves after you trade

If that were the whole story, every market maker would be rich. The catch is what happens after a fill. When a taker
buys from you, you are now short. If the taker knew something, the price rises, and the short loses more than the
spread earned. So the question is not "how wide is the spread" but "how wide is the spread compared with how far the
price moves, on average, in the direction of the trades".

*Trades, Quotes and Prices* (eq. 17.13, PDF p. 345) gives the gain of a patient market maker, per unit traded:

::: {.eq speak="a market maker's gain per unit traded is half the average spread, less how far the price eventually moves in the direction of the trades"}
$$\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{G}]}{\nu_0 T} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[s]}{2} - \mathcal{R}_\infty$$
:::

In it, [$s$]{speak="s"} is the spread and [$\mathcal{R}_\infty$]{speak="R infinity"} is the long-run *impact*: after a buy, how far the mid ends up above
where it was, on average, and the same for sells with the sign flipped (the book's eq. 1.9, PDF p. 35). Half the
spread is what each fill earns at once; the impact is what the market takes back later. On the large stock markets
the book studies, the two nearly cancel, and without the exchange's rebates the plain strategy loses (§17.2.2):
making markets is a competitive business with thin margins.

Both sides can be measured from the data alone, before writing any bot, with the impact after 50 ticks standing in
for the long run. On Prosperity 3's round 1 the margin is clearly positive: about 0.9 of a tick (a credit) a unit on
Kelp and 1.4 on Resin, and trades barely move the price at all. On ABIDES it is negative, −0.32 of a tick (a cent) a
unit, because its trades move the price by 1.3 ticks within 50 ticks
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Does market making pay here, by the textbook's test?"; "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}.
That one measurement says whether plain market making can work on a market at all. Prosperity is the easy case, the
textbook's "zero-intelligence" market where takers know nothing; chapter 5 is about the other kind.

### So where does the income come from?

Three things decide it, and you control only some of them:

- **How much uninformed flow there is,** traders who cross the spread for reasons that don't predict the price. They
  are the market maker's customers. You can't create them.
- **How many others compete for them.** The story: a second bot at your price takes a little under half. Quoting a little better
  than the others wins the trades, but each step inside the spread gives away margin.
- **How well you avoid the informed.** Quoting further from the fair, pulling quotes when the book looks dangerous,
  or skewing them against your position (moving both quotes so the side that adds to it is the less attractive)
  all trade a little income for safety. Chapter 5.

One caution about @fig-copies: between them the copies make a little more than one bot alone (83 and 86 thousand
against 73). Don't read anything into that: a replay can't let the market react to two bots instead of one, so the
total isn't something a real market would pay. Read each copy's share, which is what would be scored.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Measuring [$\mathbb{E}[s]/2 - \mathcal{R}_\infty$]{speak="half the spread less the impact"} from the data is estimating a baseline's expected reward before you
train anything: if it is negative, no amount of tuning a plain market maker will fix it. It breaks in one place: it
is measured on other traders' trades, and your quotes change who trades with you. A bot that quotes tighter than
everyone gets more of the informed flow too.
:::

- Copies and rivals in one market: `arena.backtest BOT DAYS --vs OTHER_BOT` (repeatable).
- The rows: "Does market making pay here, by the textbook's test?", "The template against copies of itself", "The
  template against the teams' P4 traders in one market".
:::

:::
